He transferred to USC in 1967, led the nation in rushing with 1,543 yards, and won the national title. In 1968, he won the Heisman Trophy with a record margin of 1,750 points.

name: Henryk Górecki
milestone_by_age_26: Had a monographic concert devoted entirely to his music at the Silesian State Philharmonic in Katowice in February 1958 at age 24, and completed his First Symphony in 1959 at age 25, marking his arrival as a leading figure of the Polish avant-garde.
early_history_summary: Górecki was born in a small Silesian village to a railway worker father and a pianist mother who died when he was two. Despite being discouraged from music, he began violin lessons at age 10. He taught school from 1951-53, then studied at the State Higher School of Music in Katowice from 1955-60 under Bolesław Szabelski. His first public performances in 1958 led to a Warsaw Autumn Festival debut and international recognition.
family_context_summary: Born to Roman Górecki, a railway station worker and amateur musician, and Otylia, a pianist who died when Henryk was two years old. The family lived modestly in rural Silesia. His father and stepmother discouraged his musical interests.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother played piano but died when he was two; father was an amateur musician who worked at a railway station. No professional music domain transfer documented due to early mother's death and family discouragement.
primary_early_advantage_tags: orphaned mother, rural poverty, self-taught beginnings, Polish cultural thaw, Warsaw Autumn Festival, mentor Szabelski
evidence_summary: Górecki grew up in modest circumstances in rural Silesia, losing his pianist mother at age two and being discouraged from music by his father and stepmother. He persisted, beginning violin lessons at 10, teaching school to support himself, and studying at the Academy of Music in Katowice under Bolesław Szabelski. The post-Stalin cultural thaw of 1956 opened opportunities for avant-garde exploration, and by 1958 he had a monographic concert at the Silesian State Philharmonic and debuted at the Warsaw Autumn Festival, establishing himself as a leading Polish avant-garde composer by his mid-20s.
starting_point: Born in a small village in Silesia, Poland to a railway worker father and pianist mother who died when he was two; family lived modestly and discouraged his musical interests.
current_position: Died November 12, 2010 at age 76 in Katowice, Poland from lung infection complications. Final role: composer and former professor of composition at the Academy of Music in Katowice.

name: Lidiya Skoblikova
milestone_by_age_26: Won two Olympic gold medals at the 1960 Squaw Valley Winter Olympics in the 1500m and 3000m speed skating at age 21, setting a world record in the 1500m; later won four gold medals at the 1964 Innsbruck Olympics at age 25.
early_history_summary: Skoblikova was born in Zlatoust, Soviet Union, to a working-class family. She trained at Burevestnik and later Lokomotiv sports societies. At age 17, she set national 1500m and 3000m records. She qualified for the Soviet team at 19 in 1959, placing third at the world championships. At the 1960 Olympics, she won gold in the 1500m (with a world record) and 3000m. In 1963, she won the world all-around championship winning all four distances, and in 1964 she won all four Olympic golds at Innsbruck.
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class family in Zlatoust, Soviet Union, with three sisters and one brother. Her husband Aleksandr Polozkov was a competitive racewalker and national team member who also coached her during parts of her career.

evidence_summary: Skoblikova was born into a working-class family in Zlatoust in the Ural region of the Soviet Union. She set national records at age 17 and qualified for the Soviet team at 19. The Soviet state sports system, through Burevestnik and Lokomotiv sports societies, provided the institutional pipeline for her development. She won two Olympic golds at 21 in 1960 and an unprecedented four golds at 25 in 1964, becoming the first Winter Olympian to win four individual golds at a single Games. Her husband, a racewalker, also served as her coach during parts of her career.

name: Peter Bondra
milestone_by_age_26: Scored five goals in a single NHL game on February 5, 1994 at age 25, becoming the fastest player to record five goals in a game; was also an NHL All-Star in 1993 and won the Czechoslovak league championship in 1988 at age 20.
early_history_summary: Bondra was born in Lutsk, Ukrainian SSR, to a Slovak father and Polish mother. The family moved to Poprad, Czechoslovakia when he was 3. He played one season for HK Poprad in the lower ranks and transferred to VSŽ Košice in the First Division at 18 in 1986. He won the Czechoslovak league championship with Košice in 1988. Drafted by the Washington Capitals in 1990 (156th overall), he made the team immediately as a rookie with no minor league time. He scored 5 goals in a single NHL game on Feb 5, 1994.
family_context_summary: Born in Lutsk, Ukrainian SSR to a Slovak father who had moved from Czechoslovakia at 16, and a Polish mother. Family moved to Poprad, Czechoslovakia when Peter was 3. His father died in 1982 when Peter was 14. His older brother Juraj also played hockey professionally and won a championship with Košice.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older brother Juraj played hockey professionally for VSŽ Košice on defense, having won a championship the year before Peter joined. Father died when Peter was 14, creating financial hardship. No parental hockey expertise documented.

evidence_summary: Bondra was born in the Soviet Union to a Slovak-Polish family that moved to Czechoslovakia when he was 3. His father died when he was 14, creating hardship. He joined VSŽ Košice's First Division team at 18, where his older brother Juraj already played, and won the league championship at 20. Despite being drafted 156th overall by the Washington Capitals in 1990, he made the NHL team immediately as a rookie. By age 25, he had scored five goals in a single NHL game and was an All-Star. His path was marked by self-created repetition in Czechoslovak leagues and the sibling connection with his brother at Košice.
